The attack failed, and I got a second Bower witness the verifier did not have. FIRST WITNESS, the one the verifier named: the DLI scan of the Penguin Bower setting at archive.org (in.ernet.dli.2015.507721). Read this run, it gives the title page as Penguin Books in association with Hamish Hamilton, translated by Anthony Bower, the translation first published by Hamish Hamilton in 1953, foreword by Herbert Read, and it prints section 1 THE REBEL closing on 'I rebel - therefore we exist.' with the next section head '2 METAPHYSICAL REBELLION' following. SECOND WITNESS, which I went and got because one scan of one setting is thin: the complete chapter 1 text hosted at thephilosopher.net (The-Rebel-Albert-Camus-1.pdf), which I downloaded and extracted with pdftotext. It ends: 'In our daily trials rebellion plays the same role as does the "cogito" in the realm of thought: it is the first piece of evidence. But this evidence lures the individual from his solitude. It founds its first value on the whole human race. I rebel therefore we exist.' and then stops. Two independent transcriptions of Bower, two different settings, and in both the sentence under test is the LAST sentence of chapter 1. The locator 'ch. 1, the closing sentence' is correct and is the strongest part of the proposal.

A REAL DIVERGENCE I FOUND, WHICH DOES NOT BITE. The two Bower settings are not the same text in the run-up to the line. The Penguin scan reads 'But this clue lures the individual from his solitude. Rebellion is the common ground on which every man bases his first values.' where the other reads 'But this evidence lures the individual from his solitude. It founds its first value on the whole human race.' That is the Hamish Hamilton 1953 setting against the revised Knopf setting that Vintage carries, both of them Bower. I chased it because a divergence two sentences from the shipped line is exactly where translation drift hides. It does not touch the shipped line: the closing sentence is word for word identical in both, so 'trans. Anthony Bower, 1953' covers whichever copy a reader picks up, and the source line is right not to name a publisher.

THE DASH. The Penguin OCR renders it 'I rebel - therefore we exist' and the philosopher.net plain text drops the dash entirely, 'I rebel therefore we exist.' Neither is evidence against the em dash: the same philosopher.net transcription renders every printed dash in the chapter as a double hyphen ('the rebel--once he has accepted the motives'), and OCR of an em dash as a spaced hyphen is routine. The em dash is what the printed Bower carries and what the line is known by. I also checked the house rule and the house practice. Rule 5 bans the em dash in the SOURCE and the NOTE only, and this source line has none. js/data-year-classics.js already ships seventeen em dashes inside quotations, among them Dostoevsky's 'a new story—the story of the gradual renewal of a man' and Nietzsche's 'virtue, art, music, dancing, reason, spirituality—anything whatever'. So the em dash inside the quotation is both the edition's wording and settled house practice.

ONE EVIDENCE-LEVEL ERROR, NOT A SHIPPING ERROR. The evidence field claims 'p. 28 in the Penguin setting'. The same scan the verifier cites puts chapter 1 at pp. 19 to 27 with the next section head on p. 29, so the closing sentence is on p. 27 and p. 28 is the blank verso. The page number is not in the source line, so nothing false reaches the card, but the evidence should say p. 27 rather than p. 28 if it is going to say a page at all.

EVERY OTHER GATE. shipped.js: shipped [], near [], albert camus at 1 of 3 (January), cap 3, not banned. Attribution is not in dispute and is on no trap in the misattribution list; the list's Camus-adjacent entries are Sartre's 'Hell is other people' and Nietzsche's 'God is dead', neither of them this. No speaker to name: this is Camus in his own voice in a book-length essay, not a character. Scope: L'Homme revolte 1951, Bower 1953, well before 1999, not scripture, not film, not lyric, not proverb, not business, not oratory. Publishable: no wound, no dying, no atrocity, nothing needing a warning. Source line is 81 characters, leads with the author's name, carries no dash anywhere, and puts work, then locator, then translation in parentheses, which is the order rule 5 asks for. Tag Philosophy is the form of the work; Essay is arguable, since the French subtitle calls it an essay, but The Rebel is shelved and taught as philosophy and Philosophy is not wrong. Theme fit is good rather than perfect: it is a solidarity line before it is a courage line, but 'in our daily trials' is literally the clause that sets it up, and a line that answers trial by saying you are not alone in it is a July line at six in the morning.
